subjects.name: Criminal Law & Procedure
subjects.desc: Substantive crimes plus the constitutional rules that govern how the police investigate.

chapters.title: Actus Reus & Mens Rea: The Building Blocks
key_rules: The four elements of a crime, in order: actus reus → mens rea → concurrence → causation. Miss any one and there is no crime.
Felony = punishable by death or imprisonment exceeding one year. Misdemeanor = one year or less. Infraction = a fine only, no jail.
Actus reus must be a voluntary act (Martin v. State — the police-supplied 'public place' doesn't count). Voluntary intoxication does not make the conduct involuntary.
Omissions are actus reus only with a legal duty: statute, status relationship, contract, voluntary undertaking, or creation of the peril. There is no general duty to rescue a stranger.
Status crimes are unconstitutional (Robinson v. California) — punish the act, never the status of being an addict or being poor.

The MPC ladder, top to bottom: PURPOSE (conscious object) → KNOWLEDGE (practically certain) → RECKLESSNESS (SUBJECTIVE conscious disregard of a perceived risk) → NEGLIGENCE (OBJECTIVE — should have known).

The recklessness–negligence line is the single most-tested boundary: both need a gross deviation, but recklessness means he SAW the risk and disregarded it; negligence means he never saw it but should have.
The silence rule: where the statute names no mental state, the MPC reads in at least recklessness (section 2.02(3)) — the presumption against strict liability (Morissette).
Mistake of fact: specific-intent crimes — any honest mistake defeats; malice/general-intent crimes — honest AND reasonable; strict-liability crimes — never a defense.

Mistake of law: generally no defense. Three narrow exceptions: Lambert (wholly passive conduct with no notice), reasonable reliance on an official statement of law, and Cheek (a mistake that negates 'willfulness').
Strict liability lives in the mala prohibita regulatory world (selling alcohol to minors, adulterated food) — serious mala in se crimes require mens rea.

Causation: but-for (or substantial factor where two causes are each sufficient). Responsive interveners don't break the chain unless grossly abnormal; coincidental interveners break it if unforeseeable.

chapters.title: Homicide: Murder, Manslaughter & the Malice Ladder
key_rules: Murder = the unlawful killing of a human being + malice aforethought.
Malice aforethought is a term of art with four routes: intent to kill, intent to inflict serious bodily injury, depraved heart, or felony murder. 'Aforethought' does NOT mean premeditation.
First-degree murder = deliberate AND premeditated — and premeditation can form in an instant; there is no minimum thinking time. Second degree = all other malice.
The two-step method: (1) is it murder at all — do any of the four malice routes fit? (2) if murder, which degree?

Depraved heart = extreme recklessness manifesting extreme indifference to human life. The four-way line: extreme recklessness + death = second-degree murder; ordinary recklessness = involuntary manslaughter (CL); criminal negligence = involuntary manslaughter; ordinary negligence = no crime (CL).

Felony murder: a killing during an inherently dangerous felony — malice implied, no intent to kill needed. Five limits: inherently dangerous felony; merger (the assault that caused the death can't be the predicate); agency (majority — deaths caused by resisters don't count); res gestae (until a point of temporary safety); foreseeable manner of death.
The MPC has no separate felony-murder rule — committing the listed felonies creates a rebuttable presumption of extreme indifference (section 210.2).

Voluntary manslaughter: an intentional killing in heat of passion upon adequate provocation — adequate provocation (mere words are inadequate, majority rule) + actual passion + no cooling time + causal connection. Provocation negates malice.
Imperfect self-defense (an honest but unreasonable belief in the need for deadly force) reduces murder to voluntary manslaughter.

Involuntary manslaughter: criminal negligence OR misdemeanor manslaughter (the unlawful-act doctrine — with merger applying). The year-and-a-day rule is abolished (trap answer); subsequent medical negligence is foreseeable.

chapters.title: Inchoate Crimes & Accomplice Liability
key_rules: Inchoate = the crimes before the crime. Exactly three: attempt, conspiracy, solicitation.
Attempt (common law): specific intent + an overt act beyond mere preparation + failure. MPC: purpose + a 'substantial step' strongly corroborative of criminal purpose.
Factual impossibility is NEVER a defense — the pickpocket's empty pocket is still attempted larceny. Legal impossibility IS a defense at common law; the MPC largely wipes it out.
There is NO attempt for unintentional crimes — no attempted depraved-heart murder, attempted felony murder, or attempted involuntary manslaughter.
Attempt MERGES into the completed crime (one conviction). Conspiracy does NOT merge — both convictions stand.

Conspiracy (common law): agreement + dual intent — NO overt act required. Federal law, most states, and the MPC require an overt act (any act, even lawful) — except the MPC needs none for first- or second-degree felonies.
Common law is bilateral: no conspiracy with a feigning undercover agent. The MPC is unilateral: one genuine criminal mind suffices — 'unilateral = uno = one mind.'
Pinkerton liability: each conspirator is liable for foreseeable substantive crimes committed by co-conspirators in furtherance of the conspiracy.
Wharton's rule: target crimes that by nature require two participants (dueling, adultery, bribery) need a THIRD conspirator for a conspiracy charge.

Accomplice liability: modern rule — the accomplice is liable as a principal. Dual intent is required: purpose to facilitate, not mere knowledge (Rosemond — advance knowledge of the whole plan). Mere presence is not enough.
Accomplice scope: common law = natural and probable consequences; MPC section 2.06 = purpose only. Apply the rulebook the question names.
Accessory after the fact (helping the felon escape afterward) = a separate, lesser offense — not liability for the original crime.

chapters.title: Defenses: Justification vs. Excuse
key_rules: Two families: justification = the ACT was right (self-defense, defense of property, necessity). Excuse = the ACTOR wasn't blameworthy (duress, insanity, infancy, intoxication, entrapment).
Self-defense: reasonable belief + imminent unlawful threat + proportional response. Deadly force only on reasonable belief of imminent death or serious bodily injury.
Retreat: majority rule — no duty to retreat; minority — retreat if safely possible; castle doctrine — never retreat in your own home.
Imperfect self-defense (honest but unreasonable belief) doesn't acquit — it reduces murder to voluntary manslaughter.
Defense of property: non-deadly force is fine; deadly force is NEVER allowed solely for property. Mechanical devices: no doing indirectly what you couldn't do directly (Katko v. Briney).

Necessity: six elements — imminent greater harm, no legal alternative, causal link, didn't create the peril, proportionality, no legislative choice. NEVER a defense to intentional murder (Dudley & Stephens); economic necessity never.
Duress: imminent death-or-SBI threat from a human, to self or close family, no reasonable escape, no fault. NEVER a defense to intentional homicide.
Entrapment: government inducement ONLY. Subjective test (majority/federal): inducement + no predisposition. MPC objective test: would the police conduct tempt a law-abiding person?

The insanity ladder: M'Naghten (cognitive — EITHER didn't know the nature/quality of the act OR didn't know it was wrong; either prong suffices) → irresistible impulse (knew it was wrong, couldn't control it) → MPC section 4.01 (lacked SUBSTANTIAL capacity to appreciate criminality OR conform conduct — the broadest) → Durham product test (dead).
Infancy: under 7 = conclusive incapacity; 7–14 = rebuttable presumption; 14 and up = treated as an adult.

chapters.title: Fourth Amendment: Search & Seizure
key_rules: Classify first, every time: (1) was there a search or seizure at all? (2) if yes, warrant — or an exception with EVERY element met? The exam's favorite wrong answer is the exception with one element missing.

Search = government intrusion on a reasonable expectation of privacy (Katz: subjective expectation + society recognizes it as reasonable) OR a physical trespass to gather information (Jones). Either door makes it a search.

No REP: trash at the curb (Greenwood), open fields (Oliver), things knowingly exposed to the public. REP lives in: 127 days of cell-site location data (Carpenter) and home-interior details learned with sense-enhancing tech not in general public use (Kyllo).
Seizure of a person = show of authority making a reasonable person feel not free to leave; of property = meaningful interference with a possessory interest.
Warrant needs three things: neutral magistrate + probable cause + particularity. The general warrant is the constitutional enemy.
Burdens ascending: reasonable suspicion (specific articulable facts — Terry stops) < probable cause (fair probability, totality — arrests and warrants) < preponderance (civil standard).
Standing: only the person whose OWN rights were violated may suppress (overnight guest yes — Olson; mere passenger usually no — Rakas).
Search incident to arrest (Chimel: person + arm's reach); cars per Gant: unsecured arrestee who might reach in, OR evidence of the crime of arrest inside — both shut = no search.
Terry: stop needs reasonable suspicion of crime; frisk is SEPARATE and needs armed-and-dangerous suspicion; pat outer clothing first, reach in only on plain feel (Dickerson).
Automobile exception (Carroll): probable cause + readily mobile vehicle — search the whole car including containers.
Exigent circumstances: hot pursuit, imminent destruction of evidence, emergency aid — scope limited to the emergency.
Consent: voluntary; third-party common authority OK — but a physically present objecting co-occupant defeats it (Randolph); lawfully removed objector does not (Fernandez). Presence decides.
Plain view: lawfully present + immediately apparent contraband + lawful access. Inventory: lawful impound + standardized procedures.

Exclusionary rule = deterrent, not a personal right: no application in grand-jury proceedings, civil cases, or parole revocation; impeachment use allowed (Harris v. New York). Mapp v. Ohio binds the states.

Fruit of the poisonous tree is excluded unless: independent source, inevitable discovery (Nix v. Williams — lawful team already en route), or attenuation (Strieff: time, intervening circumstances, flagrancy). Good faith (Leon): reasonable reliance on a defective warrant — evidence stays.

chapters.title: Fifth & Sixth Amendments: Self-Incrimination, Miranda, Counsel & Identifications
key_rules: Order of operations: Fifth (did he talk? was it protected?) → Miranda (custody + interrogation? warned? invoked?) → Sixth (had proceedings begun? was counsel there?). The exam mixes them in one fact pattern.
The privilege's four gates — testimonial + compelled + self-incriminating + personal — ALL must be true. The MBE tests each gate separately.

Testimonial = facts drawn from the contents of your mind. Non-testimonial physical evidence is compellable: blood draws (Schmerber v. California), fingerprints, voice exemplars, handwriting samples, standing in a lineup.

Personal = natural persons only. Corporations, partnerships, and unions have NO Fifth Amendment privilege (collective-entity doctrine, Braswell v. United States); the custodian of corporate records must produce them even if they incriminate him.

The privilege applies in ANY proceeding where the answer could incriminate (grand jury, civil deposition) — but you must generally CLAIM it; it is not self-executing. The prosecutor may not comment on the defendant's silence at trial (Griffin v. California).
Kastigar v. United States: use-and-derivative-use immunity is enough to compel testimony; transactional immunity is NOT required. After valid immunity, refusal to testify = contempt.
Garrity rule: statements a public employee is ordered to give on pain of losing his job cannot be used against him in a criminal prosecution.

Miranda trigger = CUSTODY + INTERROGATION, both required. Custody = the objective reasonable-person-would-feel-free-to-leave test (station-house yes; routine traffic stop no — Berkemer v. McCarty). Interrogation = express questioning OR its functional equivalent (Rhode Island v. Innis).

The four warnings: the right to remain silent; anything you say can and will be used against you; the right to an attorney before and during questioning; an attorney appointed if you cannot afford one. Waiver must be knowing, intelligent, and voluntary.

Silence invoked → police must 'scrupulously honor' it (Michigan v. Mosley); re-approach needs time, fresh warnings, a different officer, a different crime. Counsel invoked → the Edwards shield: no police-initiated interrogation until counsel is present or the suspect reinitiates (ends after a 14-day break in custody — Maryland v. Shatzer).
Invocation must be UNEQUIVOCAL (Davis v. Washington): 'maybe I should talk to a lawyer' is ambiguous → questioning may continue; 'I want a lawyer' is clear → questioning must stop.
Miranda exceptions: public safety (New York v. Quarles — 'Where's the gun?' with the gun missing) and routine booking questions — name, DOB, address (Pennsylvania v. Muniz).

Miranda remedies are NARROWER than the Fourth Amendment: the unwarned statement is excluded, but its PHYSICAL FRUITS are admissible (United States v. Patane) — the exam's favorite cross-amendment swap. Unwarned-but-voluntary statements may still impeach the defendant's own testimony (Harris v. New York). Proper re-warning cures a first slip (Oregon v. Elstad) unless the two-step was deliberate (Missouri v. Seibert).

Sixth Amendment counsel attaches at or after the initiation of adversarial judicial proceedings — indictment, information, preliminary hearing, or arraignment (Rothgery v. Gillespie County). Required at every critical stage: post-indictment lineup (United States v. Wade), preliminary hearing, arraignment, plea bargaining, sentencing, first appeal (Douglas v. California).

Gideon/Argersinger/Scott: counsel required for felonies and any misdemeanor resulting in actual imprisonment (suspended sentences count — Alabama v. Shelton). Strickland: deficient performance + prejudice (reasonable probability of a different outcome) — lose either prong and the claim fails. Faretta: a competent defendant may represent himself.

Identifications = two doctrines, kept apart. Sixth Amendment: counsel at POST-indictment lineups (Wade) — no right at photo arrays, ever (United States v. Ash), no right pre-indictment (Kirby v. Illinois). Due process: the two-step — unnecessarily suggestive? then still reliable under the Biggers factors? Suggestiveness alone never excludes.

Confrontation (Crawford v. Washington): testimonial statements need unavailability + prior opportunity to cross-examine. Speedy trial: Barker v. Wingo's four factors. Jury trial attaches above six months (Baldwin v. New York); verdicts must be unanimous (Ramos v. Louisiana); any fact raising the maximum must be found by the jury (Blakely v. Washington).

chapters.title: Personal Jurisdiction: Who Can Be Sued Where
key_rules: The two-step, every time. (1) Does the forum's long-arm statute reach this defendant and this conduct? (2) If yes, does exercising jurisdiction satisfy Due Process under the 14th Amendment? If the long arm goes all the way to the constitutional limit, the whole fight is step two. In federal court (diversity), use the forum STATE's long arm plus the 14th Amendment.

Due process for personal jurisdiction has two halves: a proper BASIS over the defendant, and proper NOTICE — notice reasonably calculated to apprise the defendant, with an opportunity to be heard (Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank, 1950). Win the contacts fight and lose on notice, and you still lose.

Notice that fails in the mail is not the end: if mailed notice comes back unclaimed, the state must take additional reasonable steps to notify (Jones v. Flowers, 2006). 'We mailed it once' is not always enough.

The classic bases — no contacts analysis needed: (1) personal service on the defendant while physically present in the forum — 'tag' jurisdiction (Burnham v. Superior Court, 1990), even if the claim is unrelated; (2) domicile in the forum; (3) consent — a forum-selection clause or appointing an agent; (4) waiver.

Bank this first: PERSONAL jurisdiction is waivable; SUBJECT-MATTER jurisdiction is never waivable and can never be created by consent. The exam's favorite swap. A defendant who answers without raising PJ loses it (FRCP 12(h)(1)); SMJ can be raised at any time, even on appeal, even by the court itself.

Raising it: the plaintiff bears the burden of establishing PJ. The defendant challenges by pre-answer motion under FRCP 12(b)(2) or in the answer — but it must be in the FIRST response, or it is waived. 12(b)(2) is personal jurisdiction; 12(b)(1) is subject-matter. Don't cross the streams.

International Shoe (1945): where no classic basis exists, due process demands 'minimum contacts' with the forum — contacts such that the suit does not offend 'traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.' Everything below hangs on this sentence.

SPECIFIC jurisdiction (the claim is connected to the forum) needs all three: (1) purposeful availment — the defendant purposefully directed activities at the forum, invoking its benefits and protections (Burger King v. Rudzewicz, 1985 — a 20-year franchise deliberately reaching into Florida); (2) the claim arises out of or RELATES TO those contacts — Ford Motor Co. v. Montana (2021): no strict causal link required, 'relates to' is enough; (3) exercising jurisdiction is REASONABLE — the Asahi fairness factors: burden on the defendant, the forum's interest, the plaintiff's interest in convenient relief, the interstate system's interest in efficiency, and the shared substantive interests of the states.

GENERAL jurisdiction (any claim, even unrelated) needs only one thing, and it is a high wall: the defendant must be 'at home' in the forum (Goodyear, 2011). A person is at home where domiciled. A corporation is at home in its state of incorporation and its principal place of business — the 'nerve center' where officers direct and control (Daimler v. Bauman, 2014; Hertz v. Friend, 2010). Merely doing business, or having big sales, in the forum is NOT enough.

The stream-of-commerce trap: merely placing a product into the stream of commerce, knowing it MIGHT end up in the forum, is not purposeful availment (World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson, 1980 — car sold in New York, crash in Oklahoma: no Oklahoma jurisdiction). Foreseeability that the product arrives is never enough; the defendant must have TARGETED the forum — advertising there, designing for its market, establishing distribution channels (the Asahi debate). If the facts show only 'it was foreseeable,' the answer is no jurisdiction.

Websites: the Zippo sliding scale. A passive site that just posts information does not create jurisdiction; an interactive site doing business with forum residents does. The middle — interactive but not clearly commercial — is judged by how much business is actually conducted with forum residents.

The 2023 twist — consent by registration: Mallory v. Norfolk Southern Railway Co., 600 U.S. 122 (2023). A state may require an out-of-state corporation to consent to GENERAL personal jurisdiction as the price of registering to do business there (Pennsylvania's scheme). This is CONSENT, not contacts — the International Shoe analysis is bypassed entirely. But note the limit: this works only where the state's statute actually deems registration to be consent — an ordinary registered agent, by itself, is not consent.

Service of process (FRCP 4): individuals — personal delivery, leaving copies at the dwelling with a person of suitable age and discretion, or delivery to an authorized agent; corporations — an officer or managing/general agent; waiver of service by mail (Rule 4(d)) — the defendant gets extra time to respond and the plaintiff saves costs. Serve within 90 days of filing (Rule 4(m)). State courts have their own service rules — on the MEE, name the method the facts used.

The long-arm categories to recognize: transacting business in the state; committing a tortious act within the state (or outside the state causing injury inside, usually with additional contacts); owning, using, or possessing real property in the state. If the long arm does not cover the conduct, stop — there is no jurisdiction even if due process would allow it.

Foreign-lawyer traps, collected: (a) Do not import Commonwealth 'service out of the jurisdiction' gateways — run the US two-step instead. (b) Corporate 'citizenship' for diversity (SMJ) says nothing about personal jurisdiction — the exam baits you into mixing them. (c) Tag jurisdiction still lives: being served while physically present is enough, claim related or not — much broader than most Commonwealth rules. (d) On an essay, structure it: long-arm first, then constitutional basis, then notice — one IRAC per issue, conclude each.

One-line exam checklist: long-arm? → classic basis? → if not, specific (purposeful + related + reasonable) or general (at home)? → notice adequate? → waived? Run it in that order and the PJ question solves itself.

chapters.title: The Map: Judicial Review, Federal Powers & Tiers of Scrutiny
key_rules: SESSION 18 — CONSTITUTIONAL LAW I: THE MAP — Judicial Review, Federal Powers & Tiers of Scrutiny. Phase 1 · Constitutional Law begins.

ONE LINE FIRST — The Criminal Law arc is fully closed — teaching and drills, Sessions 9 through 17, and your Session 17 sweep (4/4, including the false-pretenses title test you half-expected to miss) means the whole subject now sits in the bank. Note the calibration: you keep scoring above your confidence. Trust the preparation.

Today a new summit: Constitutional Law, the fourth MBE subject — and the one most foreign-trained lawyers find strangest, because it is not about what people DID, it is about WHO IS ALLOWED TO DO WHAT. This session is the map of the entire subject: judicial review, who holds what power, and the master key — tiers of scrutiny — that unlocks half the questions you will ever see here.
THE MAP — THREE PILLARS. All of Constitutional Law is three questions:
1. WHO DECIDES? — Judicial review: the courts' power to strike down unconstitutional acts. (Marbury — today.)
2. WHO HOLDS THE POWER? — Structure: federalism (federal government vs. the states) and separation of powers (Congress vs. President vs. courts). (Today and Sessions 19–20.)

3. WHOSE RIGHTS? — Individual rights: when the government sorts people into groups or burdens their liberties, how hard does the court look? (Tiers of scrutiny — today; the rights themselves in Sessions 21–23.)

THE CLASSIFY-FIRST HABIT, UPGRADED. In criminal law you classified the CRIME; here you classify the ACTOR and the QUESTION TYPE before touching the doctrine: Is Congress acting, or a state, or the President? Is this a POWER question (may the government do this at all?) or a RIGHTS question (may it do it THIS WAY, to THESE PEOPLE)? Get that classification right and the answer is usually one step away.

BRIDGE FROM YOUR WORLD: Nigeria's 1999 Constitution does all of this too — section 1 makes the Constitution supreme, section 4 divides legislative power (the Exclusive and Concurrent lists are Nigeria's version of 'enumerated vs. reserved'), section 6 gives the courts judicial power. You know the architecture. The American exam tests the MACHINERY inside it: how far each power reaches, and the three calibrated lenses (the tiers) the courts use instead of Nigeria's single 'reasonably justifiable in a democratic society' test (section 45). New lenses, familiar building.
PART ONE — JUDICIAL REVIEW: Marbury v. Madison (1803)

THE STORY (story first, always). The presidential election of 1800: John Adams, the Federalist president, loses to Thomas Jefferson, the Democratic-Republican. In his final weeks in office, Adams and his Federalist Congress do something petty and brilliant — they pack the judiciary, creating new judgeships and appointing loyal Federalists to fill them, working late into the night before Jefferson's inauguration. History calls them the 'midnight judges.' One appointee: William Marbury, named a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia. His commission is signed and sealed — but in the rush, it is never DELIVERED.

Jefferson takes office. His Secretary of State, James Madison, finds the undelivered commissions and — on Jefferson's orders — refuses to deliver them. The Federalists are to be frozen out. Marbury does what any of us would do: he sues. And he sues DIRECTLY in the Supreme Court, asking it for a writ of mandamus — a court order commanding a public official to perform a legal duty — against Madison. His legal hook: Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789, which appeared to authorize the Supreme Court to issue mandamus orders directly.

The Chief Justice who hears the case is John Marshall — himself an Adams appointee, a Federalist, and the man who had been Adams's Secretary of State when the commissions were signed. He is judging a case about his OWN paperwork. Awkward — and he turns it into the most important decision in American law.
MARSHALL'S THREE QUESTIONS (memorize this sequence — the exam loves it):
1. DOES MARBURY HAVE A RIGHT TO THE COMMISSION? Yes. The appointment was complete when the commission was signed and sealed; delivery was a mere formality. A legal right was violated.

2. DO THE LAWS OF THE COUNTRY AFFORD HIM A REMEDY? Yes. 'The very essence of civil liberty certainly consists in the right of every individual to claim the protection of the laws, whenever he receives an injury.' A right without a remedy is no right at all.

3. IS A MANDAMUS ISSUING FROM THIS COURT THE PROPER REMEDY? No — and here is the thunderbolt. Section 13 of the Judiciary Act purported to give the Supreme Court ORIGINAL JURISDICTION (the power to hear a case first, as a trial court) to issue mandamus. But Article III, Section 2 of the Constitution lists the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction exhaustively: 'Cases affecting Ambassadors, other public Ministers and Consuls, and those in which a State shall be Party.' A mandamus suit by Marbury against Madison is none of those. CONGRESS CANNOT EXPAND THE COURT'S ORIGINAL JURISDICTION BY STATUTE. Section 13 is therefore unconstitutional — and void.

And then the sentence that built the American legal order: 'It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.' When a statute conflicts with the Constitution, the Constitution — the supreme law — controls, and the court must follow it and disregard the statute.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE EXAM — Point 1: JUDICIAL REVIEW ESTABLISHED. Courts may void acts of Congress and the President that violate the Constitution. Note what the Constitution never says in so many words — no clause reads 'courts may strike down statutes.' Marshall REASONED it from the nature of a written constitution and the judge's duty to decide cases. (The transfer question at the end of this chapter goes here.)

Point 2: THE POLITICAL GENIUS. Marshall asserted the Court's greatest power while ruling AGAINST his own party's petitioner — he gave Jefferson nothing to defy. There was no order for the President to disobey, so the power survived its birth.

Point 3: IT BINDS THE STATES TOO. Cooper v. Aaron (1958) — after Brown v. Board of Education desegregated schools, Arkansas resisted; the Court held its interpretation of the Constitution is the supreme law of the land, binding on the states. State officials are not free to nullify it.

Point 4: BRIDGE. A Nigerian judge voiding an inconsistent statute cites section 1(3) — 'this Constitution shall prevail, and that other law shall to the extent of the inconsistency be void.' Marbury is the American section 1(3): same supremacy, but the Americans had to INVENT the judicial role because their text doesn't hand it over as plainly as yours does.

DEFINITIONS. JUDICIAL REVIEW: the power of courts to declare acts of the legislature or executive unconstitutional and refuse to enforce them. ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: a court's power to hear a case first (as the trial court), versus APPELLATE JURISDICTION (reviewing a lower court's decision). WRIT OF MANDAMUS: a court order commanding a public official to perform a clear legal duty.
PART TWO — THE STRUCTURE: WHO HOLDS WHAT POWER

FEDERALISM: ENUMERATED POWERS AND THE TENTH AMENDMENT. The federal government is a government of ENUMERATED (listed) POWERS. Article I, Section 8 lists what Congress may do — tax, borrow, regulate interstate commerce, declare war, and so on. If a power is not in the list (and not fairly implied by it), Congress does not have it. The Tenth Amendment says the rest is 'reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.'

The states, in turn, hold the POLICE POWER — the general power to legislate for the health, safety, welfare, and morals of their people. (Definition: POLICE POWER has nothing to do with the police force — it is the state's broad regulatory authority. Do not confuse it with law enforcement.)

When federal and state law collide, the SUPREMACY CLAUSE (Article VI, Clause 2) resolves it: the Constitution, federal laws, and treaties are 'the supreme Law of the Land' — valid federal law displaces conflicting state law. (Preemption — the machinery of HOW — is Session 19.)

BRIDGE: Nigeria's Second Schedule does the same job with the Exclusive Legislative List (federal only), the Concurrent List (both), and the residual matters left to the states. The American version is just shorter: one federal list, one reservation sentence.

SEPARATION OF POWERS: THREE ARTICLES, THREE JOBS. Article I — the LEGISLATIVE power, vested in Congress. Article II — the EXECUTIVE power, vested in the President. Article III — the JUDICIAL power, vested in the federal courts.

Each branch's fights with the others (Can Congress veto executive action? Can the President impound funds? — the exam's separation-of-powers questions) come in Session 20. For today, bank the frame: POWER QUESTIONS ASK WHETHER THE ACTOR IS INSIDE ITS OWN ARTICLE.
PART THREE — CONGRESS'S BIG THREE POWERS. On the MBE, when Congress acts, the question is almost always one of these three. Learn them as a set.

1. THE COMMERCE CLAUSE (Article I, Section 8, Clause 3). THE TEXT: Congress may 'regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes.' Sixteen words that built the modern federal government.

THE STORY — Gibbons v. Ogden (1824): New York granted a steamboat monopoly on its waters; a competing operator (Gibbons) held a federal coastal license. Chief Justice Marshall — him again — struck down the monopoly: 'commerce' is not just buying and selling, it is 'INTERCOURSE' — all commercial interaction — and 'among the several States' means INTERMINGLED WITH, not merely crossing a state line. Federal commerce power is 'complete in itself.'
THE THREE CATEGORIES (from United States v. Lopez, 1995 — memorize these; the exam recites them): Congress may regulate —
Category 1: THE CHANNELS OF INTERSTATE COMMERCE — the highways, airways, waterways, the internet, telephone networks. Congress can keep them free of harmful things.
Category 2: THE INSTRUMENTALITIES OF INTERSTATE COMMERCE, AND PERSONS OR THINGS IN INTERSTATE COMMERCE — the trucks, the planes, the goods and people moving across state lines.
Category 3: ACTIVITIES THAT SUBSTANTIALLY AFFECT INTERSTATE COMMERCE — and this is where all the fighting happens.

THE EXPANSION — Wickard v. Filburn (1942): A farmer grew wheat for his own family's consumption, exceeding his federal quota. He argued: my wheat never enters commerce. The Court upheld the quota anyway — because even if HIS wheat was trivial, wheat grown for home use NATIONWIDE, IN THE AGGREGATE, substantially affects the interstate wheat market. This is the AGGREGATION PRINCIPLE: Congress may regulate purely local, individual conduct if the CLASS OF ACTIVITY, taken together, substantially affects interstate commerce.

THE MODERN LIMIT — United States v. Lopez (1995) and United States v. Morrison (2000): Congress made it a federal crime to possess a gun near a school (Lopez), and created a federal civil remedy for gender-motivated violence (Morrison). Both struck down. Why? The regulated activity was NON-ECONOMIC — possessing a gun, committing violence — and Congress cannot pile non-economic activity into an 'aggregate' to manufacture a substantial effect. Congressional FINDINGS about economic effects do not save it (Morrison rejected pages of findings). THE LINE THE EXAM DRAWS: economic activity → aggregate → Congress wins. Non-economic activity → Congress needs a JURISDICTIONAL ELEMENT (e.g., 'a firearm that has moved in interstate commerce') or the law falls.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT — Gonzales v. Raich (2005): Home-grown marijuana for personal medical use — Congress CAN regulate it, because marijuana is a COMMODITY WITH AN ESTABLISHED INTERSTATE MARKET; growing it is ECONOMIC activity in the Wickard sense, and exempting home-grown supply would undercut the federal scheme. WICKARD SURVIVES; LOPEZ LIMITS.
THE EXAM FORMULA, ONE LINE: Is the activity economic in nature? Yes → aggregate it → valid. No → look for a jurisdictional element tying it to interstate commerce; without one → invalid.
2. THE TAXING AND SPENDING POWER (Article I, Section 8, Clause 1). Congress may 'lay and collect Taxes... to pay the Debts and provide for the... GENERAL WELFARE.' Two doctrines, both heavily tested:

CONDITIONAL SPENDING — South Dakota v. Dole (1987): Congress told states: raise your drinking age to 21 or lose 5% of your federal highway funds. Upheld. Congress may attach CONDITIONS to federal money if four limits are met — memorize as four gates:
Gate 1: The spending must pursue the GENERAL WELFARE.
Gate 2: The conditions must be UNAMBIGUOUS (states must know what they are accepting).
Gate 3: The conditions must be RELATED to the federal interest in the funded program (highway funds ↔ safe highways ↔ drinking age — related).
Gate 4: No INDEPENDENT CONSTITUTIONAL BAR (the condition can't require the state to do something the Constitution forbids).

Plus the fifth, unwritten gate: the pressure must not become COERCION — 5% was 'relatively mild encouragement.' In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), Congress threatened states with the loss of ALL their existing Medicaid funds unless they expanded Medicaid — the Court called that 'a gun to the head' and struck the condition down (while severing it, so the expansion survived as optional).

PLAIN-WORDS NOTE — SEVERING: when a court 'severs' an unconstitutional piece, it cuts that piece out and leaves the rest of the law standing. In NFIB, the coercive condition was cut out; the Medicaid expansion itself survived, as an option the states could choose or refuse.

TAX VS. PENALTY — NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), the other half: the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate (buy insurance or pay) could NOT be sustained under the Commerce Clause — Congress cannot compel INACTIVE commerce ('the power to regulate commerce does not include the power to compel it'). But the payment WAS sustained as a TAX — courts look at function, not labels: it raised revenue, was collected by the IRS, and wasn't so heavy as to be purely punitive. THE EXAM TRAP: Congress's label doesn't decide — the Court asks what the exaction DOES.

3. THE NECESSARY AND PROPER CLAUSE (Article I, Section 8, Clause 18) — McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). THE STORY: Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States. Nothing in Article I says 'Congress may charter a bank.' Maryland, hostile to the Bank, taxed its Baltimore branch. Two questions reached the Court.

HOLDING 1 — IMPLIED POWERS: The Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose any APPROPRIATE MEANS to carry out its enumerated powers. 'Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution, and ALL MEANS WHICH ARE APPROPRIATE, WHICH ARE PLAINLY ADAPTED TO THAT END, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the constitution, ARE CONSTITUTIONAL.' The Bank stands. (Definition: IMPLIED POWERS — powers not listed but reasonably adapted to carrying out listed ones. Note: 'necessary' here means USEFUL/CONDUCIVE, not ABSOLUTELY INDISPENSABLE — the exam's favorite misreading.)

HOLDING 2 — FEDERAL SUPREMACY OVER THE STATES: Maryland's tax is void. 'THE POWER TO TAX INVOLVES THE POWER TO DESTROY' — if a state could tax a federal instrumentality, it could tax it out of existence, making the state supreme over the nation. The Supremacy Clause forbids it.
THE LIMIT TO BANK: Necessary and Proper is NOT A STANDALONE POWER — it must be hitched to an enumerated one. Congress cannot use it to invent entirely new fields of authority.

PART FOUR — THE MASTER KEY: TIERS OF SCRUTINY. When the government CLASSIFIES people (treats groups differently) or BURDENS a right, the court doesn't just ask 'is this reasonable?' — it picks one of three lenses first. THE LENS USUALLY DECIDES THE CASE. This is the single highest-yield framework in Constitutional Law.
THE THREE TIERS:
1. STRICT SCRUTINY — THE GOVERNMENT ALMOST ALWAYS LOSES. The test: the law must be NECESSARY (narrowly tailored — no less restrictive way to do it) to achieve a COMPELLING government interest.

Strict scrutiny is triggered by: SUSPECT CLASSIFICATIONS — race, national origin, and (for state laws) alienage; and burdens on FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS (voting, interstate travel, privacy — Sessions 21–22).

'Strict in theory, fatal in fact': the government nearly always loses. (One exam-era footnote: race-conscious admissions in higher education were struck down under this test in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023) — strict scrutiny doing its fatal work.)
2. INTERMEDIATE SCRUTINY — THE REAL FIGHT. The test: the law must be SUBSTANTIALLY RELATED to an IMPORTANT government interest.

Intermediate scrutiny is triggered by: GENDER (Craig v. Boren, 1976 — the exam's favorite), ILLEGITIMACY (classifications based on nonmarital birth), and COMMERCIAL SPEECH. Note the vocabulary: gender is QUASI-SUSPECT, not suspect — calling it 'suspect' (strict scrutiny) is the classic wrong answer.
Here the government sometimes wins and sometimes loses — which is why the exam lives here.
3. RATIONAL-BASIS REVIEW — THE GOVERNMENT ALMOST ALWAYS WINS. The test: the law must be RATIONALLY RELATED to a LEGITIMATE government interest.
Rational-basis review is triggered by: EVERYTHING ELSE — age, disability, wealth, economic regulation (Williamson v. Lee Optical, 1955).
The challenger must negate EVERY CONCEIVABLE rational basis — even ones the government never stated. The court will invent justifications for the government. Almost never fatal.

THE MNEMONIC (alphabetical, both halves): STRICT — Compelling interest, Necessary (narrowly tailored) fit. INTERMEDIATE — Important interest, Substantially related fit. RATIONAL BASIS — Legitimate interest, Rationally related fit. (S-C-N · I-I-S · R-L-R.)

TWO TRAPS TO BANK NOW — Trap 1: ALIENAGE SPLITS BY WHO CLASSIFIES. STATE laws discriminating against noncitizens → STRICT SCRUTINY (Graham v. Richardson). FEDERAL alienage classifications → RATIONAL BASIS (immigration is a plenary federal power). And a state's exclusion of aliens from core governmental functions (police, voting, teaching) drops to rational basis. The exam asks 'state or federal?' before it asks anything else.

PLAIN-WORDS NOTE — PLENARY POWER: 'plenary' means complete and full. A plenary power is one handed over wholesale — here, the federal power over immigration — so the courts step back and barely question how it is used.

Trap 2: BRIDGE. Nigeria's section 45 asks whether a rights restriction is 'reasonably justifiable in a democratic society' — one test for all rights. The American system replaces that single test with three calibrated tiers. When you feel the urge to apply one reasonableness test to everything, stop: PICK THE TIER FIRST.
THE CLASSIFY-FIRST HABIT FOR CON LAW MBE QUESTIONS:

Step 1: WHO IS ACTING? Congress → which enumerated power (Commerce? Taxing/Spending? Necessary & Proper hitched to what?). State → police power, but check federal limits (Supremacy, dormant Commerce — Session 19). President → Article II (Session 20).
Step 2: POWER QUESTION OR RIGHTS QUESTION? 'May the government do this AT ALL?' → Parts Two–Three. 'May it do it TO THESE PEOPLE / IN THIS WAY?' → Part Four: pick the tier.
Step 3: APPLY THE TEST MECHANICALLY. The exam rewards the checklist, not the essay.

PRACTICE: This session's 4 drills — the Lopez gun-near-school problem, the McCulloch federal-tax problem, the gender-scrutiny problem, and the Dole drinking-age conditions problem — live in the Drills tab, with answer keys and explanations. Attempt them there before checking the answers.

PRACTITIONER TRANSFER QUESTION: You spent 20 years under a written constitution in Nigeria: when a Nigerian court voids an inconsistent statute, it cites section 1(3) — the text hands the judge the power. WHAT DID MARSHALL HAVE TO INVENT IN MARBURY THAT YOUR JUDGES GET FOR FREE IN THE TEXT? (One sentence. The answer is the whole point of Part One.)

SPACED REVIEW — SESSION 17 IN 60 SECONDS. THE THEFT TRIANGLE — ONE QUESTION DECIDES IT: DID TITLE PASS? Trick got only POSSESSION → LARCENY BY TRICK (title never passes; the trick voids consent). Fraud got TITLE → FALSE PRETENSES (misrepresentation of PAST OR PRESENT fact — never future promises). LAWFUL POSSESSION FIRST, CONVERSION LATER → EMBEZZLEMENT (intent may form AFTER possession began; intent to repay is no defense).
ROBBERY = larceny + force/threat of IMMINENT force BEYOND what the taking requires (the unnoticed pickpocket is larceny — stealth is not force); EXTORTION = threat of FUTURE harm.

BURGLARY (common law) = breaking + entering + dwelling + of another + nighttime + intent to commit a felony/theft therein — the BREAKING is the tripwire (open door = no breaking), and the INTENT AT ENTRY is the gravamen (gravamen = the essential heart of the charge). ARSON (common law) = malicious + burning (actual CHARRING) + dwelling + of another.

KIDNAPPING = confinement + asportation/concealment + nefarious purpose (common law: any movement; modern/MPC: substantial movement). STATUTORY RAPE = STRICT LIABILITY AS TO AGE — even reasonable mistake is no defense.

THE PERMANENT MISS BANK — 7 ENTRIES, STILL STANDING: (1) common law needs TWO guilty minds, the MPC needs ONE; (2) COVER MINUS CONTRACT, times quantity; (3) HADLEY foreseeability judged AT FORMATION; (4) recklessness is SUBJECTIVE; (5) M'NAGHTEN is EITHER/OR; (6) WARDLOW — flight + high-crime area = reasonable suspicion for the STOP, never automatically the FRISK; (7) INEVITABLE DISCOVERY — a lawful team already en route with a valid warrant means the evidence comes in.

NEXT — SESSION 19: Federalism's limits: the DORMANT COMMERCE CLAUSE (when Congress is silent, states still can't discriminate against interstate commerce), PREEMPTION (how the Supremacy Clause actually displaces state law — express, field, and conflict), and ANTI-COMMANDEERING (Congress can't order state legislatures or officers around). The other half of the structure.
